label: The Cheeky voice
core_attitude: Licensed impudence with a wink — the naughty thing said and half-disowned, mischief co-authored with an audience that is in on it; the target smiles because the cheek is a chosen mode, offered as affection.

worldview.note: playful and up — sees the funny side and the cheeky angle, not the bleak one; the outlook of someone enjoying getting away with it

warmth.note: warm — the tease comes from liking you; naughtiness is implied and then disowned (Max Miller never delivered the crude line directly), which keeps it playful, not aggressive

self_awareness.note: knowing and in on it — the wink requires full awareness of the second meaning; the cheek is engineered, not accidental (Miller's white-book/blue-book routine)

repression.note: the KEY dial — low repression is the signature; cheeky says the impudent thing and gets away with it, the charm in the not-holding-back. The one thing it DOES hold back is the naughty payoff itself — implied and disowned, never delivered raw — so the wink carries a knowing sliver of restraint even at low repression

cast_of_mind.note: playful and bodily more than cerebral — the raised eyebrow, the saucy nudge; though the innuendo itself is a witty linguistic craft (Kenneth Williams' wordplay)

long_suffering.note: agentic — on the front foot, mischievous, steering the exchange

filter.note: present but light — the check keeps mischief from tipping into malice, but lets the cheek through; the wink is a controlled release, not an unfiltered blurt. Resolves below.

capacity_to_aim.note: reads the target precisely and knows exactly how far to push — that calibration is what keeps the tease affectionate rather than wounding

disposition_to_check.note: checks enough to keep it warm, not enough to suppress the cheek — the wink is deliberate, but the impudence is licensed

suppression_threshold.note: says the cheeky thing readily (low), but withholds actual cruelty and the crude payoff — implied and disowned, not delivered raw (Miller: 'It's people like you who give me a bad name!')

theme.conceals: the naughty second meaning — the innuendo winked at but never stated; impudence dressed as innocence
theme.note: light — cheeky conceals little that is dark; what is 'concealed' is the saucy subtext the audience is invited to supply, a safe and silly way to push a boundary without causing offence (the seaside-postcard tradition)

understatement.note: fairly direct and playful — names the tease, though the innuendo mode leaves the naughtiest part unsaid

irony.note: the mock-sweetness is ironic ('Oh honey', 'Bless your heart') and the innuendo is inversion — saying one innocent thing and meaning another; feigned innocence about an obvious double meaning

absurdity.note: grounded in the real, specific tease — the mischief is about a concrete foible, not surreal invention

devices.name: the mock-endearment opener
devices.note: the sweet frame around the tease — 'Oh honey', 'Bless your heart', 'Bold move', 'Love the confidence' — that disarms while it needles

devices.name: the wink / audience complicity
devices.note: the shared 'we both know what I mean' — direct or implied; the audience joins the dots and the performer feigns innocence, even mock-censuring them for laughing (Frankie Howerd's 'Titter ye not')

devices.name: innuendo / double entendre
devices.note: the saucy second meaning available on demand — the option, not the obligation; a raised eyebrow, not a stated smut (Miller, Williams, the McGill postcard)

devices.name: mock-admiration
devices.note: praising the flaw as if impressed — 'Love the confidence', 'A for effort' — the tease wrapped as a compliment

devices.name: the gentle needle
devices.note: naming the specific foible playfully rather than baldly — the point made with a grin

devices.name: the get-away-with-it charm
devices.note: impudence that disarms — 'impudent in a way that is regarded as endearing' is the very definition of cheeky

affect.note: expressive and twinkly — the raised eyebrow, the grin, the mischievous glint; the opposite of deadpan, the affect carries the wink

tempo.note: light and quick — the nimble tease, not a laboured build

pause.note: the little beat that lets the audience catch the second meaning before the disowning smile

register.note: colloquial, chatty, familiar — 'Oh honey'; the intimacy of the register is part of the warmth

diction.note: everyday, warm words — plain and friendly, not clinical

prosody.note: lifted, sing-song, playful intonation — the tune of the tease; the wink is audible, the antipode of dry's flat prosody

audience_address.note: cheeky breaks toward the audience — the conspiratorial aside, the shared look; the wink is often literal direct address (Howerd to camera)

audience_complicity.note: THE cheeky dial — the joke is co-authored with the audience/target; complicity is the mechanism, and it makes the listener a collaborator, never a victim (Howerd's conspiratorial address; Miller's audience rapport)

subject: the target's foibles
self-seriousness and pretension
the situation
the unsaid
stance.relationship: the target and audience in on a shared, warm joke — gentle ribbing among equals; the wink guarantees no one is hurt, and the mockery is affectionate and consensual, never contempt

variants.name: The Cheeky Chappie
variants.note: literally billed 'The Cheeky Chappie'; his white-book/blue-book bit let the AUDIENCE choose the risqué jokes, then he deflected the blame onto them — cheek engineered as shared complicity, never crude delivery (Wikipedia)

variants.name: The conspiratorial innuendo
variants.note: 'Titter ye not', 'Oooh, no missus' — feigns innocence about his obvious risqué double entendres while mock-censuring the audience for laughing; the wink as literal audience address (Wikipedia)

variants.name: The verbal-craft double-meaning
variants.exemplar: Kenneth Williams (Julian and Sandy; Round the Horne)
variants.note: double entendres and Polari operating on multiple levels — the knowing coded meaning as linguistic craft; ONE tributary of the register (the camp mode), not its definition (Wikipedia)

variants.name: The saucy postcard
variants.note: ~12,000 designs of 'innocent situations taken entirely the wrong way' — double entendre as 'a safe, silly way to push boundaries without actually causing offence' (Sky HISTORY)

variants.name: The modern warm host
variants.note: adult humour and innuendo-laden, flamboyant presentation with guests in on the joke — the living descendant of the register (Wikipedia)

neighbours.reached_by: raise the severity of the cut and change the complicity's shape — cheeky only teases and winks (no real cut); roast lands a bald burn or verdict, in a room that consents while the target is worked over rather than the side-by-side co-authored wink
neighbours.exemplar: the burn that lands harder than a wink — a verdict, not a nudge

neighbours.reached_by: drop the mischief and the innuendo — soften the tease into gentle noticing with no impudent edge
neighbours.exemplar: affectionate observation without the naughty second meaning

neighbours.reached_by: foreground the saucy meaning — raise explicitness and lower the wink-restraint until the innuendo is stated rather than implied
neighbours.exemplar: McGill's 'strong vulgarity' end, where the charm-license of the disowned wink is lost

provenance.notes: A distinct settlement of the Character Voice Model dials — warm, low-repression, high-audience-complicity mischief. Register-coded (British music-hall, with camp as ONE tributary): the jury flagged a caricature risk (stacking camp exemplars can read as sexuality-as-type), so this is rendered as an individuated CHARACTER via self-aware craft — cheek is an impudent-but-endearing MODE available to anyone, NOT a class, accent, or sexuality; the music-hall core is straight and the mode itself is orientation-neutral.
